ios.desc:
Wiktionary Reader is a fast, focused way to explore Wiktionary — the free, collaborative, multilingual dictionary — on iPhone and iPad.

SEARCH 198 LANGUAGE EDITIONS
Look up words in English, Japanese, French, German, Chinese, and nearly 200 other Wiktionary editions. Reorder the language list to keep your favorites on top, and hide the ones you don't need.

QUICK LOOKUPS
Matching entries appear as soon as you search, and recent results are cached so repeat lookups show up instantly. Tap the dice button to discover a random entry and pick up a new word.

A BETTER READING VIEW
• Search an entry's title again with a single tap
• Translate an entry into your preferred language with the globe button (powered by Google Translate)
• Follow links freely with Home, Back, and Forward buttons
• Open an entry in Safari or share it
• Dark Mode support
• Save images from entries to Photos

BOOKMARKS AND HISTORY
Bookmark the words you want to come back to. Every entry you open is added to your history automatically. Search and reorder both lists, and set how many items each one keeps. Export your bookmarks to a file and import them on another device.

TWO-COLUMN LAYOUT ON LARGER SCREENS
On an unfolded iPhone Duo or on iPad, search results appear on the left and the entry on the right, so you can move from word to word without losing your place. Fold your iPhone Duo and the app switches to a single column automatically. You can turn the two-column layout off in Settings.

AVAILABLE IN 50 LANGUAGES
The app's interface is localized into 50 languages, including English and Japanese.

Wiktionary Reader is not an official app of the Wikimedia Foundation. Wiktionary content is written by its contributors and is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License and other licenses. An internet connection is required to search and read entries.

quotes.text:
I frequently use Wiktionary on desktop. I find it invaluable for tracing certain elements of etymology, but still largely prefer Etymonline.

It's worth noting that I access these things most frequently on mobile, so an app (with a clean, ad-free, streamlined UI) is paramount.

Your comment sparked me to seek out whether Wiktionary has an app— and apparently someone has built this iPhone app for a reader view, which at first use appears identical to the desktop view: https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/wiktionary-reader/id984975341
quotes.story_title: Ask HN: In which areas have you compared 3+ tools and formed strong preferences?
